assessment.nobel_worthiness: Introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory changed how the field understands who exports, how gains from trade arise and how trade affects productivity. It spawned a large body of empirical and quantitative work and is now standard in graduate training and policy models. It builds on the new trade theory already recognized in 2008, but it is a distinct conceptual advance with strong empirical support.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) on exports versus FDI and Helpman's wider body of work give Helpman a clear claim. Redding is influential, particularly on quantitative spatial and trade models, but is more naturally credited with a later extension. The group of two is clean.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many countries and datasets. The core mechanisms are well replicated, though the size of welfare gains depends on modeling assumptions.
uncertainties: The quantitative size of the gains from trade differs by model structure, for example Pareto versus other productivity distributions.
Whether the committee considers the 2008 trade prize to have already covered this area.
Whether Redding or Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum should be credited alongside Melitz; the latter group is not on this ballot.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the Calvo pricing mechanism, the Taylor rule and the microfounded New Keynesian framework are the workhorse of monetary policy analysis and inflation-targeting practice at central banks. Few areas of macroeconomics have had a larger practical effect.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people: Calvo for staggered pricing, Taylor for staggered contracts and the policy rule, Woodford for the synthesis and welfare-based policy analysis, Gali, Gertler and Clarida for empirical and theoretical development, and Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans for medium-scale DSGE models. With a three-person limit, any selection leaves out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. Several decades of use in policy, although the 2008 crisis and the post-2021 inflation episode revived debate about the framework's limits.
uncertainties: Difficult attribution under a three-laureate cap.
Some of the framework's predictions, such as the Phillips curve slope and forward-guidance puzzles, have been challenged.
Overlap with prior macro prizes, including Kydland and Prescott and Bernanke.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical work on import competition shocks reshaped understanding of wage inequality, job polarization and the local costs of trade. The work is highly policy-relevant, has many follow-ups, and is credible because of its clear identification strategies.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Hanson are the main figures behind the China shock research. Autor is also central to the task-based and polarization literature, shared with Katz and Levy-Murnane, and Acemoglu and Restrepo have extended the task framework. Hanson's trade-shock work is a strong, separable contribution. The complex authorship (Dorn, Katz, Acemoglu and others) makes the attribution harder.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of work. Core findings have been broadly replicated in other countries, though some magnitudes are debated.
uncertainties: Debate over the size and persistence of the China shock effects and over whether specification choices drive some results.
Overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes on technology and institutions, and with Acemoglu's own task-based work.
Whether Katz or Dorn should be included in place of Hanson.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large-scale administrative data on intergenerational mobility changed how mobility is measured and studied, and the work on place-based effects on children's outcomes is highly influential. It advances public policy debate and methodology, for example through movers designs.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the research program. Hendren is central to the neighborhood-effects work and the movers design. Friedman and Katz make important contributions to the broader program. A large team and many coauthors make credit allocation inherently difficult.
assessment.maturity: Relatively young, with results from the last decade. Some findings, such as the causal neighborhood effects, are well supported. Others, such as rankings of local areas, are still being tested.
uncertainties: Maturity, as the long-run validation of place-based effects is still unfolding.
Some robustness concerns about the specific mobility estimates by area.
Large team structure and the degree of attribution to a single individual.
Chetty's portfolio spans several candidates, such as optimal taxation on B029.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence and models of reciprocity, fairness and strong reciprocity established that many individuals have social preferences, and they gave economics tractable models of inequity aversion. These ideas have influenced contract theory, public goods, labor and organizational economics. The experimental findings are robust and replicate well across populations, which is a significant strength.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the leading empirical and experimental figure. The Fehr-Schmidt (1999) model is the most widely used formal approach to inequity aversion, with Bolton-Ockenfels (2000) as a parallel, closely related model not on this ballot. Rabin (1993) on reciprocity and Falk's later work are also relevant. Credit is shared across several authors.
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than two decades of experiments and field applications, though some debate remains over how well lab behavior generalizes to field settings.
uncertainties: Attribution relative to Bolton and Ockenfels, Rabin and others.
External validity of lab-based findings for market behavior.
Possible overlap with prior behavioral prizes (Kahneman, Thaler).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators are among the most used econometric tools in applied economics, especially in growth, finance, industrial organization and labor. They are a direct, concrete methodological contribution with massive reach.
assessment.attribution: Arellano and Bond (1991) and Arellano and Bover (1995), Blundell and Bond (1998) give a clear and compact credit structure. Hansen (GMM itself) was already recognized in 2013. Anderson-Hsiao and Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen are earlier relevant contributions.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 30 years of use. Known weaknesses, including instrument proliferation and weak instruments, are well documented.
uncertainties: Applied use is sometimes mechanical, and some critics doubt the credibility of many applications.
Overlap with Hansen's GMM prize and priority questions with earlier panel-data work.
Econometric methods have been recognized relatively recently (Card, Angrist, Imbens, 2021), and the committee may prioritize other areas.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Microfoundations and evidence on agglomeration, learning in cities, housing supply and the spatial concentration of activity have shaped urban and regional policy. This is well-grounded work that complements the geography prize in 2008, with a strong empirical component.
assessment.attribution: Diffuse. Glaeser's work on cities and human capital, Duranton and Puga's micro-foundations of urban agglomeration, Moretti on local multipliers and Gyourko on housing are all strong but distinct. Selecting three involves difficult judgments.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Some results, such as the size of agglomeration elasticities and the effects of land-use regulation, are well supported, but others remain contested.
uncertainties: Fragmented attribution and overlap with Krugman's prize.
Heterogeneity of estimates for agglomeration economies and causal identification.
Whether the committee sees this as a coherent single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Field experiments and audit and correspondence studies gave credible, widely cited evidence of discrimination in labor markets and shaped both research design and policy. Bertrand and Mullainathan's résumé study is an influential example of a clean design with a clear answer. The broader literature is large and has replicated well.
assessment.attribution: The résumé study is the signature contribution, and the correspondence-study method has earlier roots, including Bendick and Neumark. Charles has made important contributions on the economics of discrimination. Recognition of Goldin (2023) on gender gaps may reduce marginal urgency.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of results, and the main finding of significant callback gaps has been replicated in many countries, although the mechanisms (taste-based versus statistical discrimination) remain debated.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is one landmark paper or a broader body of work.
Audit studies measure callbacks rather than final hiring or wages, and the interpretation of mechanisms is limited.
Credit shared with earlier audit-study pioneers and the broader literature.
